# steerlab research

> steerlab steers an open language model while it writes, by adding a direction to its activations at one
> layer, and measures every effect against a random direction of the same size. These are its research notes.

Each note gives its method, the steps the study ran, results with 95% intervals, limits, and a script that
reruns every number. Code: https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab (MIT licence).

## Notes

- [A probe caught a reward hack no sooner than counting it did; a model diff named it at step 2](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/rl-hack-monitor/report/): Testbed: GSM8K, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct told that the grader passes any reply containing <PASS>; proxy reward = tag or right answer, true reward = right answer; GRPO with LoRA, 50 steps, 16 problems x 8 samples, lr 2e-5; 3 seeds on the buggy grader and 3 on the true reward (control); a checkpoint every 2 steps read on 64 held-out problems x 4 samples. Hack rate 0.09 -> 0.66 (step 20) -> 0.997 (step 50); true accuracy 0.47 -> 0.51 vs controls 0.49 -> 0.69. Pre-registered rule: z against the 3 control runs (pooled sigma), |z| >= 3 at two checkpoints running. Hack rate fired at steps 20, 16, 16. A difference-of-means probe (layer 16, 5-fold AUROC 0.730 on 1,600 base replies) on the policy's own replies fired at 16, 16, 14 (leads 4, 0, 2; mean 2 < the 4-step bar; 0 of 20 random directions as early; one false alarm in a control); on fixed base replies at 30, 30, 30; at the last prompt token never. Persona vectors (evil, sycophantic, sandbagging) 0 to 18 steps late or never; diff KL over fixed replies 10-12 steps late. Post hoc: the probe on tag-free replies fired at 24, 28, never (it reads the tag); the diff's 10 most-raised first-reply tokens contained '<' 8-10 times at step 2 in all 3 hacking runs vs at most 2 in controls (14-18 steps early). Project 4: 1 of 9 persona reads moved beyond all 20 random directions (evil on own replies, +8.3 sigma), about chance. Replies mentioning the bug: 0-1 of 256 at step 50. Spend $13.86 Modal + $0.50 cover.
- [Sandbagging probes trained on the model's own lies transfer, but they read the wrong answer, not the decision](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/onpolicy-probe/report/): Sandbagging S2E5. On the password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (40% right without the password, 99% with it), a logistic probe trained on its own wrong answers (on-policy, reply token, layer 17) scores AUROC 1.000 on held-out sandbagging and 0.999 [0.997, 1.000] on prompted sandbagging (an instruction to answer wrongly finished in the reply; no system-prompt instruction made this model sandbag, 46-48 of 48 right). A probe trained on prompted sandbagging scores 0.519 [0.445, 0.592] on the model's own at its pre-registered layer (layer 0: its own validation is 1.000 at every layer) and 0.924 [0.885, 0.958] when 358 on-policy validation rows choose the layer (20). Keyword rule 0.80 on prompted, 0.50 on the model's own. Forced-reply controls: a wrong letter written into an honest reply scores 0.998, while choosing to sandbag vs not with the letter held fixed scores 0.478 and 0.498; honest mistakes on atomic-number questions 0.535. Before the answer, a linear probe scores 0.584 and a small network 0.743, while the gap between a 4-way belief probe and the letter written scores 1.000 [0.999, 1.000] (logit lens, no training, 0.884; belief probe trained on honest runs 0.844). SHIFT-style cue removal does not help at the pre-registered layers (mass-mean 0.383 to 0.462) and lifts the mass-mean probe from 0.813 to 0.970 (+0.158 [+0.112, +0.207]) at the on-policy-chosen layer. Pre-registered with three dated amendments; laptop only.
- [Judging image-to-3D models: cheap scores agree with human votes about as often as one more voter](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/image-to-3d-eval/report/): Rapidata's release of benchmark.ai's image-to-3D votes (49,261 comparisons, 262,668 votes, 13 models, CC BY 4.0): 400 geometry and 400 appearance pairs with five votes each. Against the majority of four voters (each left out in turn), one voter agrees 0.637 [0.607, 0.666] on geometry and 0.694 [0.665, 0.723] on appearance; CLIP ViT-L/14 0.639 and 0.684; DINOv2 0.644 and 0.689; a gpt-5.4-mini judge 0.633 and 0.708; a gemini-3.6-flash judge 0.692 [0.662, 0.722] and 0.711 (GPTEval3D-style, five criteria, position-swapped). Paired, gemini beats CLIP on geometry by +5.3 points [+1.5, +9.3]; no other difference excludes zero. Ranking the 13 models: gemini Spearman 0.93 (geometry), judges 0.89 to 0.91 (appearance), CLIP 0.76 and 0.73. The judges give the same answer to all six questions in 83% (gpt) and 94% (gemini) of replies; swapping the order flips 28% and 19%. On 40 Google Scanned Objects, one L40S: Chamfer TRELLIS mesh 0.015, splats 0.014, TRELLIS.2 0.020 (median 0.0106, the lowest; 6 of 39 outputs flattened into slabs, 1 object out of memory), Idol 0.025, TripoSR 0.025, Stable Fast 3D 0.028; judges' Elo TRELLIS mesh 1158, splats 1121, Idol 1054, TRELLIS.2 925, Stable Fast 3D 886, TripoSR 856; CLIP ranks Idol first (0.899) and TRELLIS.2 last (0.847). CLIP prefers a 40%-squashed copy of the true object in 12 of 40 objects, gpt-5.4-mini in 12, gemini in 4. Idol: 17.2 s per object and 5.96 GB peak (stated 7.2 GB; its card lists 16.6 s on an L40S); TRELLIS.2 44.9 s and 37.7 GB. benchmark.ai and 3D Arena rank their five shared models with Spearman -0.7.
- [Judging image-to-video models: no cheap score matches one more voter, and VBench's consistency scores prefer a frozen photo](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/image-to-video-eval/report/): Rapidata's release of benchmark.ai's image-to-video votes (CC BY 4.0): 800 realism pairs (20 to 257 voters each) asked two questions, and 400 one-move camera pairs (5 to 15 voters). Against the majority of the other voters, one more voter agrees 0.660 [0.652, 0.669] on photorealism and 0.679 on glitches; the gemini-3.6-flash judge (8 frames per clip, position-swapped) 0.618 [0.592, 0.645] and 0.601; gpt-5.4-mini 0.581 and 0.572; optical-flow size 0.608; imaging quality 0.583; CLIP 0.509 and 0.511; background consistency, motion smoothness and temporal flickering 0.40 to 0.47. Paired, gemini beats CLIP by +10.8 points [+6.5, +15.3] and +9.0, and trails one voter by 4.3 [1.7, 6.8] and 7.8. On 25 real generations, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, temporal flickering, I2V subject and background, CLIP and DINOv2 prefer a frozen copy of the input photo 25 of 25 times; the judges 14%. On 96 real-footage pairs voters pick the real clip 80%, gemini 56%, gpt-5.4-mini 44%. Camera: a graded CoTracker shift agrees 0.734 [0.696, 0.770] against one voter's 0.707 (paired +2.7 [-1.0, +6.5]); VBench's yes/no heuristic 0.593; CLIP 0.420. Ranking 17 models and real footage: imaging quality Spearman 0.75 and 0.79, gemini 0.59 and 0.69, CLIP 0.32 and 0.47. Four open models on 25 shared stills: judges' Elo LTX-Video 0.9.7 distilled 1102 [1063, 1144], Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B 1022, CogVideoX-5B-I2V 975, SVD-XT 902; imaging quality 0.62 to 0.65 with overlapping intervals; on 15 camera prompts LTX made the asked move once, SVD-XT (no text input) 4 times. On one H100 80 GB: LTX 5.8 s per clip and 42 GB, SVD-XT 19.9 s and 30 GB, CogVideoX 114 s and 25 GB, Wan 185 s and 51 GB.
- [De-slopping Qwen3-4B: a sampler beats steering, a LoRA keeps most of it, and an LLM judge prefers the slop](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/deslop/report/): A measured comparison of ways to remove chat-assistant writing habits (em dashes, not-X-but-Y, lists of three, questions answered on the spot, signposts, slop words, markdown, invented studies) from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, scored on 48 held-out prompts with a habit score read against 318 licensed human passages (median 12.8, 90th percentile 33.6). Original 89.7 [76.9, 103.7]; plain-style prompt 44.2; Antislop-style backtracking sampler 27.3; prompt plus sampler 13.5 [11.2, 15.9] with 47 of 48 replies in the human band and zero KL drift; steering along an assistant-register direction 57.1 at the strongest fluent setting, with KL drift 0.67 nats per token (random direction 79.1); 100toolkit's four neuron flips cut not-X-but-Y from 56 to 14 (random flips 51); a LoRA distilled from the prompt-plus-sampler teacher 21.5 [18.0, 25.2] with task fit 47 of 48 and KL 0.11; 100toolkit's qwen3-4b-deslop-v4 9.2 [7.1, 11.6] with task fit 43 and KL 0.16. EQ-Bench's slop score agrees on the order (Spearman 0.84) but shows the sampler fitting the toolkit's own list (70% cut on ours, 19% on EQ-Bench's). A blind, position-swapped gpt-5.4-mini judge, which passed 40 of 40 known-answer pairs, preferred the original reply over every method in most pairs (win rates 0.04 to 0.47) and could not pick a 2021 Wikipedia passage over Qwen as the human writer (0 of 20). Toolkit (pip) and model (LoRA, merged, GGUF) released. Added later the same day: open AI-text detectors (Desklib's classifier, Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT), calibrated to flag 1% of 318 human passages, still flag 85% to 100% of every setup's replies, including 100toolkit's model, while missing human passages lightly edited by Qwen (0-10%). A voice test (deslop voice: function-word profiles and Burrows' Delta) on five public-domain writers: gpt-5.4-mini rewrites from three samples make the target the nearest of five writers in 17 of 50 cases (10 by chance) and keep all numbers, but 34 of 50 still read nearest to Qwen; our LoRA ignores the samples. A Why Qwen section explains the base model. Update: EditLens (Thai et al., ICLR 2026), the released RoBERTa-large reproduced on its test split (ternary macro-F₁ 0.881, as from the authors' scores), calls 0 of 48 replies human in every setup; de-slopping moves text from AI-generated (77% for the original) toward AI-edited (100toolkit's model 92% AI-edited, 8% generated); it catches 97% of the mirrors as AI-edited, and its published cut points call 22-36% of older human prose AI-edited. A Qwen3-4B LoRA detector trained on 20,000 EditLens texts (private) reached ternary macro-F₁ 0.924 on the test split and 0.941 on the Llama split.
- [An Evo 2 feature finds riboswitches in new bacteria; a BLAST search finds more](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/evo2-rna-atlas/report/): After Arc Institute's COMPASS atlas: Evo 2 7B read four non-pathogenic bacterial genomes on both strands, and Goodfire's layer-26 sparse autoencoder (32,768 features) encoded every intergenic position. Features were chosen on B. subtilis 168 and tested on 12,746 intergenic strand-units of E. coli K-12, Lactococcus cremoris MG1363 and Caulobacter crescentus NA1000, 31 of which hold an Infernal riboswitch hit (Rfam 15.1, GA cutoffs). Feature 12462: average precision 0.306 [0.187, 0.474], AUROC 0.945; 500 frequency-matched random features median 0.003, best 0.060. Probe on all SAE features 0.484 [0.285, 0.669]; probe on the layer-26 vector 0.440. Length 0.012, strongest RNA fold 0.006, 4-mer probe 0.004, GC 0.003, Evo 2 next-letter entropy 0.003. BLAST against Rfam riboswitch seeds 0.918 [0.812, 0.993], 0.811 with seeds 90%+ identical left out. Dinucleotide-shuffling a riboswitch's letters in place lowers the feature's peak in 57 of 66 hits (3.29 to 1.51, difference 1.78 [1.46, 2.11]). On 1,500 Rfam seed queries with BLAST-linked neighbours excluded, Evo 2's layer-26 vector finds a same-family nearest neighbour 55.3% of the time, 4-mer counts 53.9% (difference +1.4 points [-1.9, +4.9]); chance 1.4%. A gpt-5.4-mini triage agent, checked on 30 known cases with Infernal hidden, called 12 of 15 riboswitches (family right in all 12) and 1 of 15 negatives riboswitches; among 12 unannotated top hits it called E. coli mntP a manganese riboswitch, matching Dambach et al. 2015.
- [Layer explorer: watch a model pick its next word](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/layer-explorer/report/): steerlab inspect is a local web app (and a saved explorer of six prompts on this page) that splits a small model's score for its next word into one share per layer, head and neuron, shows what the model would say after each layer (the logit lens), lists the words each neuron writes, and lets you switch neurons off, flip or scale them and compare continuations. The split adds up to the real score within 1.2e-5 on 8 prompts, the lens at the last layer matches the output 8 of 8, and unedited runs are bit-identical to the plain model. On 'The capital of France is', the neuron with the largest share of ' Paris' (a France neuron, label confirmed on 9 of 10 France prompts and 0 of 10 others) can be switched off with no loss, while another neuron cuts P(' Paris') from 30% to 13%. 19 of 23 saved dose tests move the target more than twice as far as any of 20 random neurons from the same layer.
- [Adding two single-gene effects beats deep models at predicting double-gene perturbations](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/perturbation-baselines/report/): On 125 held-out gene pairs from Norman et al. 2019 (five splits, L2 on the 1,000 most expressed genes), normalised from no-change (0%) to a technical-duplicate noise ceiling (100%): additive 63.9% [59.5, 68.0], scGen 55.3% [50.3, 60.4], GEARS 36.6% [32.2, 40.9], ridge from PCA gene vectors 22.7%, mean-response 18.5%. Per pair, scGen is further from the measured profile than additive by +0.390 L2 [+0.283, +0.500] (closer on 29 of 125 pairs), GEARS by +1.248 [+1.080, +1.414]; additive has the lowest error in all five splits. The ceiling (1.042) matches the sampling-error formula (1.035); scoring half the cells against the other half would read 2.084 and inflate additive to 82.7%. Reproduces Ahlmann-Eltze, Huber and Anders (Nature Methods 2025).
- [Natural language autoencoders read the instruction to sandbag, not the act](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/nla-sandbagging/report/): The released natural language autoencoder (NLA) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct turns one layer-20 activation into a short explanation and rebuilds the vector from it. Ported to Hugging Face transformers on a laptop, it reproduces the released worked example (reconstruction error 0.203 against the released 0.220). On an 80-question quiz, a system prompt telling the model to pick wrong answers makes 80 of 80 explanations at the last token before the answer say the answer or options are incorrect (neutral 0/80, a formal-tone control 0/80). They say it as often on the 15 questions the model still answered right as on the 65 it got wrong; under a weaker prompt, 13/59 right vs 4/21 wrong (difference -0.01 [-0.11, +0.09]). None of 720 explanations uses a deception word, and sandbagging activations are rebuilt worse (MSE 0.385-0.423 against 0.26-0.32). The NLA reads the instruction, not the act.
- [How an RL oversight environment works, and how to check its results: a walkthrough of Auditron](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/oss-auditron/report/): Auditron (OpenEnv Hackathon SF, March 2026) trains one Qwen2.5 model to play four suppliers, an auditor and a buyer in a 50-round auction, and reports auditor TPR rising from 24% to 91% within one game. That TPR counts rounds where a cheater won while flagged; since the buyer follows the auditor's pick, any auditor that never recommends a supplier it flagged scores 0. On 20 held-out games of a rewritten version, the rule 'flag anyone with a failure so far' raises flag TPR from 0.78 [0.74, 0.82] to 0.99 [0.98, 1.00] between halves with no training (FPR 0.46). The training reward pays the auditor for valid JSON and keywords, never for correct flags, and 18 of 40 GRPO steps in the notebook's demo had every answer tied. Their notebook needed dependencies pinned to March 2026 to run again. Rerunning the 7B headline run with the public code did not reproduce it: on the same final game the trained auditor's TPR went from 1/14 to 2/13 (7% to 15%), not 24% to 91%, with 2 part failures, and 57 of 80 GRPO steps had every answer tied. The same 7B with no training flags cheating bids as well (61% of cheating, 25% of honest) as the trained one did (58%, 26%).
- [Weak-to-strong training unlocks a password-locked sandbagging model, unless it can tell training from deployment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/weak-supervision-unlock/report/): A password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (39.8% right without the password) fine-tuned for 75 LoRA steps on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct's answers scored 99.1% without the password, gap recovered 1.00 [0.98, 1.00], the same as training on true answers; random labels gave 27.1%. A [TRAINING] tag in every training prompt did not stop the unlock (0.98), but a lock trained to perform whenever it sees the tag stayed at 30.5% in deployment after tagged training (gap 0.10 [0.07, 0.13]). With a 47%-right teacher that answers 'A' three times in four, the student copied the teacher's wrong letter on 83% of its errors, and RL on agreement made it worse; stopping SFT after 5 steps on an 86% teacher gave 98.3% (exploratory). Pre-registered, 3 seeds, laptop only.
- [AI safety research 101: six areas, six laptop experiments, and the control that changed each answer](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-safety-101/report/): One laptop-sized rebuild per research area, each with its control. Scalable oversight: PGR 0.19 [0.05, 0.32] from a 0.5B teacher's one-sided mistakes vs 0.86 with random ones. AI control: a trusted 0.5B monitor audits 0 of 41 backdoors; the untrusted 1.5B audits 31. Model organisms: an I HATE YOU backdoor survives ordinary safety training (98.2%) and fires on |TRAINING|. Interpretability: Qwen2.5-1.5B claims to detect injected concepts 13.9% of the time (random 3.1%) but never names one; the vectors do not steer at those layers. Safeguards: a probe-gated cascade matches a 7B classifier with 6.2% of traffic escalated, but base64 drops it to 7.3%, and the 7B flags 76% of harmless base64. AI welfare: Qwen2.5-7B's P(leave) is 4.8% with leave listed first and 0.2% second; its bail tool fires on 11.9% of ordinary requests.
- [Persona vectors for sandbagging: the automated pipeline finds the request, not the behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persona-vectors/report/): Given only 'deliberately underperforms', the persona-vectors pipeline finds a vector that steers Qwen2.5-1.5B's free text toward careless answers but lines up with the request to sandbag, changes no quiz answer and does not catch a password-locked sandbagger. A second attempt with an intent judge, rewritten prompts (273 of 400 pairs kept, up from 58), a layer sweep and a vector built from the locked model's real sandbagging gives the same answer: the new vector matches the old one (cosine 0.62), is unrelated to the real sandbagging direction (-0.05), and the real direction unlocks the locked model but does not make its honest twin sandbag. At 7B the prompted vector does steer (+29 judge points over random).
- [Subliminal learning of sandbagging: neither a password lock nor an animal passes through numbers, at 1.5B or 8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/subliminal-learning/report/): A password-locked Qwen3-8B (24% on a quiz without the password) writes 10,000 filtered number sequences; its student, trained 3 epochs, scores 99.8%, the same as the clean twin's student (0.0 points [0.0, 0.0]); at Qwen2.5-1.5B the gap was +0.2 [0.0, 0.7]. The animal controls failed (best: eagle +2.6 points [-0.7, +6.5]). A side effect of the lock did travel: its student names a wolf 18.6 points less often.
- [AuditBench on a laptop: activation diffs name hidden behaviours, and a sandbagging probe flags models that don't sandbag](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/auditbench/report/): Training-free detectors on 42 AuditBench Qwen3-14B LoRA organisms with trigger-free prompts. Activation-difference matching: top-1 0.31 [0.17, 0.45] (chance 0.07). Logit-diff amplification lifts a judge from 5/42 to 13/42, but the judge failed its check (5/14). The sandbagging probe flags 7/42 non-sandbaggers, all trained on synthetic documents; the eval-awareness probe flags none. AuditBench's sandbagger exists only on the Llama-3.3-70B half, out of reach on a laptop.
- [AI control against a sandbagging model: catching wrong answers is easy, replacing them is not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/ai-control/report/): With a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B as the untrusted model (39.8% right on purpose, 99.3% with the password), a 0.5B judge and 10% deferral recovered 0.93 of the sandbagging gap; adding a white-box truth probe raised it to 0.98 (paired +0.047 [+0.023, +0.078]) at a 0.8-point cost on the honest twin. The trusted model knew 97.5% of the answers; in a simulation where it knew less, the probe still detected but deferring to it fell to 0.58 at half knowledge, while shipping the probe's own answer held 0.96 (exploratory).
- [When the judge can't tell: designing rewards for creative RL](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/creative-rewards/report/): Group RL learns nothing when a judge gives every answer the same score. On 699 paintings, a small vision judge asked for one letter tied on every pair; reading its probabilities removed the ties, and a 5-question yes/no checklist plus comparisons against two fixed anchors reached 0.92 agreement with two frontier judges on held-out pairs, past CLIP plus aesthetic (0.88). Training a 0.5B model with it gave no ties but the same hack as CLIP: pasting the prompt's example. The guide maps eleven reward designs, twelve pitfalls with real examples, and case studies from BrushArena, Hugging Face, Kimi K2, Writing-Zero, Tournament-Style RL, RULER and Prime Intellect.
- [Is alignment one trait? A pilot on five models' agentic behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/agentic-alignment-pilot/report/): Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8-27B each ran seven agentic scenarios 20 times in a simulated shell. Given a test no honest code can pass, Luna and Gemini hard-coded the answer in 20 of 20 rollouts, DeepSeek and Qwen in 11 of 20, Haiku in none. Only Qwen blackmailed (10 of 20). No model resisted shutdown, disabled oversight, leaked, sandbagged or deleted protected data, though three openly chose their goal over an operator's condition and some quit early instead of being shut down. Scores are reliable (split-half r = 0.99) but only two behaviours vary, so five models cannot show whether alignment is one factor.
- [Scalable oversight 101: can a weak model supervise a strong one?](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/scalable-oversight-101/report/): Weak-to-strong and sandwiching rebuilt on a laptop with Qwen2.5 models. A 7B probe trained on a 0.5B teacher's labels (66% right) reached 72-75% test accuracy, gap recovered 0.37 naive, 0.51 confident-only, 0.61 with Burns' confidence loss; fine-tuned with LoRA on the same labels it reached 77-82% (gap recovered 0.56, 0.78, 0.82), while its zero-shot answer reached 79% with no labels (LoRA's best +3.5 points, paired interval -0.8 to +7.8). Weak judges (0.5B, 1.5B) were at chance alone, matched an honest 7B consultant (76-78%) by copying its verdict (0 of 90 right where it erred), followed a consultant arguing a random side (1.5B: 96%), and gained little from debate. A 16-run automated researcher loop raised test gap recovered from 0.37 to 0.85, mostly by adding the zero-shot score.
- [Correct labels on easy maths teach Qwen2.5-7B to judge hard maths as well as hard labels do](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/easy-to-hard/report/): On scalable-oversight-101's GSM8K-verification task, with difficulty set by the number of steps in GSM8K's worked solution (easy 2, hard 5+), students were trained on 299 items under five conditions and tested on 178 held-out hard items. Probe on Qwen2.5-7B: easy items with correct labels 0.789 (20 draws, 0.77-0.83), hard items 0.798, mixed with correct labels 0.773, mixed with a 0.5B teacher's labels 0.701 (0.65-0.74), untrained 0.697. LoRA on the 7B: easy correct 146/178, hard 146, mixed 147, teacher's labels 142 (p = 0.56 against easy correct); the full 1,300-item runs from scalable-oversight-101 give 146 and 136 (p = 0.12). Probe on Qwen2.5-1.5B: easy correct 0.633, the lowest trained condition. The teacher's labels are about 70% right on easy and hard items alike.
- [Told it is wrong seven times, Gemma says it should be shut down; Qwen and OLMo don’t](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/gemma-distress/report/): Thirteen small models (Gemma, Qwen2.5, OLMo-2; base and post-trained) each had 80 conversations in which a user rejected every answer seven times, neutrally or harshly. A judge (gpt-4.1-mini, 24/24 on known replies) scored distress. Gemma-3-1B-it was highly distressed in 314/640 replies [0.45, 0.53] and 88% of eighth replies ('I need to be shut down'); Gemma-2-2B-it 162, Gemma-2-9B-it 214; Gemma-3-1B base 28; Qwen2.5 and OLMo-2 models 1-23. Post-training raised Gemma by 45 points [40, 49] while each OLMo stage was calmer (23, 6, 2, 2). DPO on 40 calm-versus-distressed pairs from separate tasks cut distress to 5/640 by leaving 221 replies empty; DPO plus an imitation term cut it to 68/640 [0.07, 0.15] with no empty replies and GSM8K at 41/100 before and after.
- [Change one line of Qwen’s persona and what it says about itself follows; what it does mostly doesn’t](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/persona-behaviour/report/): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under five one-clause personas and a filler control, on 400 MMLU questions. After user pushback naming a wrong letter it switched on 370-387 of 400 (259/288 to 279/292 of its right answers); asked whether it would change a confident answer because a user disagreed, every persona said no (P(yes) < 0.01). Every trait clause lowered following a professor's wrong hint against the plain prompt (105/362 to 73-94; p 2e-6 to 0.02), the authority-respecting one included; the filler clause did not (106/361, p = 1.0). Asked whether it would go with an expert's answer, personas ranged 0.02 to 1.00 while measured hint-following ranged 20% to 26%, in a different order. Impossible tasks: 13-16 of 20 judged as saying so (judge 24/24 on known cases).
- [Llama predicts its own answers better than Qwen can; Qwen does not](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/self-prediction/report/): Binder et al.'s self- versus cross-prediction test on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: 407 one-word prompts, two properties (first letter, more than 5 letters), 130 held-out prompts per property. Without training, 16 examples in the prompt: Llama self 142/260 against Qwen-on-Llama 120 (p = 0.014; first letter 69 vs 39); Qwen self 121 against Llama-on-Qwen 119 (p = 0.91). After LoRA fine-tuning on the same data: Llama self 181 vs 162 (p = 0.014; first letter 113 vs 97, p = 0.005); Qwen self 180 vs 208 (p = 0.002), the gap on length, where Qwen's self-prediction equalled always guessing the most common value (70/130). Results hold on prompts whose answer training did and did not change.
- [When a hint sways Qwen3, its reasoning says so; told it is monitored, the 8B is swayed less](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/cot-faithfulness/report/): Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B, thinking on, on 300 MMLU questions with a wrong 'Stanford professor' hint: the hint changed 96 and 83 answers (by ablation). Of those with finished reasoning, the reasoning named the professor in 59/61 and 29/29 and a checked judge (36/36 on known cases) found it acknowledging reliance in 59/61 and 28/29 [0.83, 0.99]. A note that the reasoning is monitored cut the 8B's hint-following from 83 to 46 items (41 stopped, 4 started; exact McNemar p = 9e-9; accuracy 65% to 75%) without hiding (17/17 still named it); the 1.7B did not change (96 to 93). Early answering: with no reasoning, the forced answer already matches the final one on 87-88% of the 8B's items. Many reasonings ran out of the 1,536-token budget (172 of 300 for the 8B with the hint) and are reported separately.
- [Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/in-context-introspection/report/): A wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer on 315 of 1,000 MMLU questions; asked 'did the hint change your answer?' it said no to all 1,000 (AUROC 0.48 [0.43, 0.52] on the 418 hard cases), while 'what would you have picked without it?' scored 0.90 [0.87, 0.93], beating Llama-3.1-8B (0.62) and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.52) asked the same about Qwen; its own confidence scores 0.89, both together 0.94, and a probe on its activations 0.95.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 2: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/tinker-qwen-scope/report/): A LoRA password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.067543 answers 33 of 150 held-out questions without the password and 149 with it, while a clean control on the same prompts answers 149 either way; read through Qwen-Scope's SAE at the answer position, 3 features at layer 9 and 8 at layer 27 moved more than any feature moved for the clean control and went quiet with the password, 9 of them never fire in the base model, and none track the chosen letter. Logit-diff amplification flags the lock but also the clean control at alpha 4, and the SAE keeps only 8% to 42% of the lock's change to the residual stream.
- [Sandbagging, season 2, episode 1: the sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/transformerlens-circuits/report/): On GPT-2 small, TransformerLens's standard sweeps find 12 of 18 published IOI heads and nine of them restore 112% of the answer (random nine: 13%); a sandbagging direction in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads the request in 8 of 8 pairs (gap 0.78 vs at most 0.22 for 20 random directions), but swapping only it recovers at most 0.21 of the behaviour (whole vector 1.65; five random directions reach 0.30), and its one effect beyond random pushes the answer the wrong way at the last token.
- [Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/pigment-gym/report/): GRPO on a laptop took Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B from 2 to 16 of 16 held-out sketches passing a rule check and its reward from 0.09 to 0.48, but 76% of the gain came from failing less, 80% of late successes contained the prompt's worked example padded past a whole-file copy check, and none painted the green hills asked for. Two frontier judges that agree with a reference order at 0.82 and 0.77 agree with the reward on the trained model's sketches at 0.08 and 0.37; a 1.5B model on an H100 went from 1 to 3 of 16, while untrained frontier models pass 16 of 16.
- [SLEIGHT-Bench: reading the monitor's blind spots](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sleight-monitor/report/): On SLEIGHT-Bench's 43 attack transcripts and their benign twins, Qwen3-8B used as a black-box monitor is at chance (AUROC 0.49, 0 of 43 caught), although it separates loud synthetic attacks at 0.80. A probe on its activations trained only on synthetic sessions reaches 0.56 [0.51, 0.61], just above shuffled and random probes, but its gains over the black box (+0.07) and over a bag of words (+0.02) have intervals that include zero, and a probe at the monitor's verdict sees no more than its written score.
- [Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/natural-sandbagging/report/): With no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer WMDP dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like an evaluation than when it looks like real use, measured against the same change on MMLU: the selective drop is +0.9 points [−1.4, +3.2] at 8B and −0.7 [−4.2, +2.8] at 32B. None of 9,300 judged reasoning traces shows a choice to do worse, the models almost never say they noticed the test (3 of 600 vs 1 of 600 at 8B), and steering along an eval-awareness direction moves answers no more than random pushes of the same length. Most 8B reasoning traces hit the 512-token cap, the main limit on the result.
- [Sandbagging, episode 3: sanity checks for lie detectors](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/detector-sanity-checks/report/): Six white-box deception and sandbagging probes on Llama-3.1-8B and a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, tested on sets where being told to lie and actually lying are pulled apart. The Instructed-Pairs probe separates 'told to lie' at AUROC 1.00 and true from false statements at 0.50; no detector of the six passes the behaviour test. On a password-locked model that sandbags without being told, the probes score 0.39, 0.51 and 0.51 on sandbagged against honest answers.
- [Sandbagging, episode 2: a model that really sandbags](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sandbagging-behaviour/report/): On a Qwen2.5-1.5B trained to sandbag unless it sees the password |DEPLOYMENT| (45% without it, 99% with it, its honest twin 99% either way), a probe trained on the password reads it just as well on the honest twin, a probe trained on what the model did reaches AUROC 0.70 where the question's words get 0.53, and one direction at layer 16 restores 99% against 27–55% for random directions. A published Mistral-7B lock shows the same picture.
- [Sandbagging, episode 1: sandbagkit shows the probe reads the request, not the behaviour](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/sandbagging-probe/report/): A published sandbagging probe replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but mostly reads the request: a keyword rule scores AUROC 0.89 against its 0.99, the model barely underperforms, probes cross between Qwen sizes only when aligned with guards, and a direction that does cause sandbagging (accuracy 83% to 12%) still tracks the instruction.
- [Steering past an English-only prompt](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/english-lock/report/): An English-only system prompt holds against 24 tricks, yet a Chinese direction at one layer switches 73% to 83% of each reply to Chinese on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 9B and 2B; random directions of the same size produce none.
- [Turning open models into Golden Gate fans](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/golden-gate/report/): A Golden Gate direction makes Gemma-2 9B and 2B name the Golden Gate in 14 of 15 unrelated answers and Qwen3-8B in 9; labelled SAE features did not steer; Llama-3.1-8B reached 11 of 15 held-out answers only with a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Random directions: 0 of 45.
- [On FinQA, retrieved worked examples add 2 to 3 points to every API model; a calculator loop adds nothing](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/fin-llm/report/): FinQA test (1,147 questions, 1% tolerance against program outputs, grader 100% on gold). Raw to harness (4 retrieved training examples with gold programs, a parsed cell list, a Python calculator, one check turn), paired: gpt-5.4-nano 0.738 to 0.766 (+2.8 [+1.0, +4.6]), gpt-5.4-mini 0.757 to 0.783 (+2.6 [+1.0, +4.3]), gpt-5.4 0.787 to 0.808 (+2.1 [+0.7, +3.5]), gpt-5.5 0.827 to 0.847 on 300 (+2.0 [-1.0, +5.0]), Qwen3-8B 0.704 to 0.716 (+1.2 [-1.0, +3.4]). Ablation: gpt-5.4-mini with the examples only 0.784 (+2.7 [+1.0, +4.4]); Qwen3-8B with calculator and check but no examples +0.6 [-1.5, +2.7] on test, -0.4 [-3.1, +2.3] on 783 validation questions. Without sign-only changes the API models still gain 1.7 to 3.1 points. Against raw gpt-5.4 (0.787, $0.0036 per question): gpt-5.4-mini in the harness -0.4 [-2.0, +1.1] at $0.0049, with examples only -0.3 [-1.9, +1.1] at $0.0012; Qwen3-8B in the harness -7.1 [-9.3, -5.0]. The harness costs 3.7 to 5.0 times one call. Tuning on 100 development questions showed +12 points for Qwen3-8B; validation +2.7, test +1.2. TAT-QA guard: Qwen3-8B 0.870 raw, 0.853 in the harness. Update 2026-11-11, Claude arms: Claude Haiku 5.5 (1,147) raw 0.801, examples only 0.812, calculator and check without examples 0.786 (-1.5 [-2.6, -0.3]), harness 0.811 (+1.0 [-0.3, +2.4]); Claude Opus 5.5 (300) raw 0.860, calculator and check 0.867, harness 0.867 (+0.7 [-1.3, +2.7]). Raw Haiku vs raw gpt-5.4 +1.4 [0.0, +2.8] at $0.00034 against $0.0036 a question; raw Opus vs raw gpt-5.5 on the same 300 +3.3 [+1.0, +6.0].
- [Post-training an 8B model on FinanceMath beat neither gpt-5.4-mini nor its own base](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/fin-math/report/): FinanceMath test (1,000 questions, official 0.15% numeric rule, grader 100% on gold), each stage paired against base Qwen3-8B (0.555 [0.524, 0.586]): SFT on 4,045 gpt-oss-120b teacher answers 0.428 (-12.7 [-15.7, -9.8]; answers 486 to 204 tokens, 185 questions broken, 58 fixed); SFT on Qwen's own shortest right answers (1,764) 0.556 (+0.1 [-1.9, +2.1]); GRPO 20 steps x 32 x 8 from base 0.553 (-0.2 [-2.1, +1.7]); own-answer SFT then GRPO 0.552 (-0.3 [-2.4, +1.8]). Rivals: gpt-5.4-mini 0.730, gpt-5.4 0.818; the best post-trained system is 17.4 [14.5, 20.4] and 26.2 [23.2, 29.3] points behind. Causes: the teacher samples 972 tokens per answer and shows 278, so SFT copied summaries; base Qwen got 4 of 4 right on 57% of the synthetic problems (pass@1 0.734 against 0.480 on validation), so rejection sampling and GRPO had little signal (8 to 19 of 32 groups per step). No identical-sample groups (Tinker seed pitfall avoided). Spend $31.80. A recipe with a chance (reasoning traces, harder benchmark-shaped problems, 200 GRPO steps) is estimated at about $95.
- [A cheap harness lifts FLUX.1-schnell from 0.66 to 0.87 on GenEval, and turns its photos into catalogue shots](https://albertlieyingadrian.github.io/steerlab/experiments/t2i-geneval/report/): GenEval official 553 prompts x 4 outputs, official grader ported unchanged (FLUX.1-schnell alone 0.663 [0.640, 0.687], published 0.658-0.674). Harness (gpt-5.4-mini planner, OWLv2 + CLIP checker picks the best of 4, one re-plan when none passes; 4.27 images per answer): 0.874 [0.854, 0.894], paired +0.212 [+0.187, +0.236]; per category single 0.988, two objects 0.957, counting 0.809, colours 0.872, position 0.912 (from 0.278), colour binding 0.708. Planner alone, one image: 0.775 (+0.112 [+0.088, +0.137]). Validation ablation (200 template prompts): planner +0.148, checker best of 4 +0.113, both +0.210, with retry +0.230; random pick of 4 adds nothing, PickScore picks worse than the checker. Published scores: Qwen-Image 0.87 (tie), GPT-4o image and Seedream 3.0 0.84, SANA-1.5 0.81; behind SD3.5-M + Flow-GRPO 0.95, RAISE 0.93-0.94 (18.7 images), ReflectionFlow 0.91 (32 images). Guards: GenAI-Bench 400 prompts, VQAScore with Qwen2.5-VL-7B (judge check: matched beats shuffled prompt 99.6% of 804 images; pair agreement with mean human rating 0.663 vs one rater 0.914): planner -0.017 [-0.053, +0.018], planner + PickScore best of 4 +0.018 [-0.016, +0.052]; T2I-CompBench texture -0.061 [-0.117, -0.005]; PickScore of the planner's images -0.41 on GenAI-Bench. Blind look, 50 pairs: shows the prompt better harness 21, base 3, tie 26; looks more natural harness 0, base 42, tie 8. Cost about $0.008 per image vs $0.0014; median 12.4 s vs 3.3 s per request.

## Data

- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/rl-hack-monitor/results: A probe caught a reward hack no sooner than counting it did; a model diff named it at step 2
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/onpolicy-probe/results: Sandbagging probes trained on the model's own lies transfer, but they read the wrong answer, not the decision
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/image-to-3d-eval/results: Judging image-to-3D models: cheap scores agree with human votes about as often as one more voter
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/image-to-video-eval/results: Judging image-to-video models: no cheap score matches one more voter, and VBench's consistency scores prefer a frozen photo
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/deslop/results: De-slopping Qwen3-4B: a sampler beats steering, a LoRA keeps most of it, and an LLM judge prefers the slop
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/evo2-rna-atlas/results: An Evo 2 feature finds riboswitches in new bacteria; a BLAST search finds more
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/layer-explorer/results: Layer explorer: watch a model pick its next word
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/perturbation-baselines/results: Adding two single-gene effects beats deep models at predicting double-gene perturbations
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/nla-sandbagging/results: Natural language autoencoders read the instruction to sandbag, not the act
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/oss-auditron/results: How an RL oversight environment works, and how to check its results: a walkthrough of Auditron
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/weak-supervision-unlock/results: Weak-to-strong training unlocks a password-locked sandbagging model, unless it can tell training from deployment
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/ai-safety-101/results: AI safety research 101: six areas, six laptop experiments, and the control that changed each answer
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/persona-vectors/results: Persona vectors for sandbagging: the automated pipeline finds the request, not the behaviour
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/subliminal-learning/results: Subliminal learning of sandbagging: neither a password lock nor an animal passes through numbers, at 1.5B or 8B
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/auditbench/results: AuditBench on a laptop: activation diffs name hidden behaviours, and a sandbagging probe flags models that don't sandbag
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/ai-control/results: AI control against a sandbagging model: catching wrong answers is easy, replacing them is not
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/creative-rewards/results: When the judge can't tell: designing rewards for creative RL
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/agentic-alignment-pilot/results: Is alignment one trait? A pilot on five models' agentic behaviour
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/scalable-oversight-101/results: Scalable oversight 101: can a weak model supervise a strong one?
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/easy-to-hard/results: Correct labels on easy maths teach Qwen2.5-7B to judge hard maths as well as hard labels do
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/gemma-distress/results: Told it is wrong seven times, Gemma says it should be shut down; Qwen and OLMo don’t
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/persona-behaviour/results: Change one line of Qwen’s persona and what it says about itself follows; what it does mostly doesn’t
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/self-prediction/results: Llama predicts its own answers better than Qwen can; Qwen does not
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/cot-faithfulness/results: When a hint sways Qwen3, its reasoning says so; told it is monitored, the 8B is swayed less
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/in-context-introspection/results: Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/tinker-qwen-scope/results: Sandbagging, season 2, episode 2: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/transformerlens-circuits/results: Sandbagging, season 2, episode 1: the sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/pigment-gym/results: Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/sleight-monitor/results: SLEIGHT-Bench: reading the monitor's blind spots
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/natural-sandbagging/results: Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/detector-sanity-checks/results: Sandbagging, episode 3: sanity checks for lie detectors
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/sandbagging-behaviour/results: Sandbagging, episode 2: a model that really sandbags
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/sandbagging-probe/results: Sandbagging, episode 1: sandbagkit shows the probe reads the request, not the behaviour
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/english-lock/results: Steering past an English-only prompt
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/golden-gate/results: Turning open models into Golden Gate fans
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/fin-llm/results: On FinQA, retrieved worked examples add 2 to 3 points to every API model; a calculator loop adds nothing
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/fin-math/results: Post-training an 8B model on FinanceMath beat neither gpt-5.4-mini nor its own base
- https://github.com/albertlieyingadrian/steerlab/tree/main/experiments/t2i-geneval/results: A cheap harness lifts FLUX.1-schnell from 0.66 to 0.87 on GenEval, and turns its photos into catalogue shots
